articles.title: EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document is the January 1990 issue, Volume 2 No. 1, of "EPHEMERIS," the official publication of the San Jose Astronomical Association. It represents a historical newsletter or journal providing information to the club's members for that specific month.

articles.title: SJAA EVENTS THIS MONTH
articles.summary: The SJAA has several events scheduled for January, including a General Meeting on January 6th featuring Kevin Medlock discussing the Large Amateur Telescope project and CCD camera. A Board Meeting will take place on January 13th, where members can suggest candidates for new board elections in February. Additionally, two star parties are planned for January 20th at Grant Ranch and January 27th at Fremont Peak State Park.

articles.title: ASTRONOMY CLASS BEGINS JANUARY 13TH
articles.summary: The San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA) is launching its Introductory Observational Astronomy class on January 13th, 1990, with Wolfgang Hanish taking over as the new teacher. The class aims to guide attendees through seasonal constellations and topics like astrophotography and telescope use, encouraging new members and those interested in amateur astronomy to attend. Jack Zeiders, the class's originator, is taking a sabbatical after three years of dedicated service.

articles.title: BRANHAM LANE STAR PARTIES
articles.summary: The SJAA is organizing a series of public star parties on various Fridays throughout the year, from January to December. Participants are encouraged to bring their telescopes and invite friends, with contact details for further information available within the issue.

articles.title: ELECTRONICS ORIENTED ASTRONOMY SEMINAR
articles.summary: The third Electronics Oriented Astronomy Seminar is scheduled for March 17, 1990, at Chapman College, Orange, California. This announcement includes a call for papers with a February 15th deadline, stressing that the seminar's occurrence hinges on sufficient program contributions. Topics like CCD camera experiments and early astro-video work with CID devices are mentioned.

articles.title: LATE BREAKING NEWS
articles.summary: Club members Jack Peterson (Treasurer) and Maria Sye were married on December 9th. The article extends well wishes to the newlyweds.

articles.title: THE EIGHTIES - LOOKING BACK
articles.summary: This article, "The Eighties - Looking Back," reviews the transformative decade of 1980-1989 in amateur astronomy, highlighting major advancements in equipment like fluorite refractors, Dobsonian telescopes, and the advent of personal computers and CCD cameras for imaging. It also recounts significant astronomical events such as Halley's Comet and the Mars opposition, alongside the growth of the SJAA including the Fremont Peak observatory and plans for a 72-inch amateur telescope. The piece concludes by listing upcoming general meetings and star parties for the San Jose Astronomical Association in January and February.

articles.title: DOUBLE, TRIPLE AND MULTIPLE STARS
articles.summary: The author recounts a Thanksgiving observing session focused on the Pleiades cluster, which brought back memories of a college project to measure its distance. The article then describes the Pleiades as a multiple star system, an open cluster of 500-1000 stars, and highlights several specific double and multiple stars within it, such as Alcyone, Taygeta, Atlas, and Pelione, that are worth observing.

articles.title: INTRODUCING AMATEUR ASTRONOMY!
articles.summary: The article highlights the past year of the SJAA's introductory astronomy class, featuring expert-led sessions on diverse topics like binocular use, astrophotography, and observing techniques, alongside hands-on experiences with telescopes. It also includes an invitation to a future class. Furthermore, the document provides detailed observing challenges and tips for resolving several difficult double and multiple star systems within the Pleiades Cluster using various telescope sizes.

articles.title: ASTRO-TIPS
articles.summary: The article describes a clever tip for astronomers: using a Telrad finder in conjunction with binoculars to easily locate celestial objects. The author, Paul M. Summers, discovered that because the Telrad projects its reticle at infinity, it can be seen through binoculars, allowing for quick and accurate centering of objects like the M8 Lagoon Nebula. The main challenge is initially locating the reticle, which is overcome by practice and adjusting brightness.

articles.title: THE CELESTIAL TOURIST SPEAKS
articles.summary: The author recounts his experience with a recently acquired 90mm fluorite refractor (Celestron SP-90F) at a public star party. He highlights its superior optical performance and portability, particularly noting how it outperformed larger telescopes under challenging seeing conditions and light pollution. While praising the refractor's exquisite views and utility as a highly portable instrument, he offers a balanced perspective, acknowledging that its cost-to-aperture ratio makes it more suitable as a secondary telescope rather than a sole primary instrument.

articles.title: GREAT RED SPOT
articles.summary: Jim van Nuland reports on recent observations of Jupiter, noting the Great Red Spot (GRS) is exceptionally colorful and easier to spot, despite a reversal in its latitudinal motion requiring earlier observation times. He also highlights a prominent dark lump in the North Equatorial Belt and the possible return of the South Equatorial Belt. The article offers practical observing tips, including recommended magnification and timing, and encourages readers to share their observations.

articles.title: COMET COMMENTS
articles.summary: The "Comet Comments" article provides updates on several comets, detailing the discovery of Comet Aarseth-Brewington by Knut Aarseth and Howard Brewington, including their observing methods and the comet's prospects for observation before perihelion. It also reports on the recovery of Periodic Comet Sanguin and Periodic Comet Tuttle-Giacobini-Kresak, noting their orbital characteristics and predicted magnitudes.

articles.title: SEEKING COMETS
articles.summary: This article analyzes the apparent motion of comets against background stars, providing crucial data for both visual and photographic comet hunters. It reports that amateur-discovered morning comets averaged 3.3 arc minutes per hour, while evening comets averaged 2.1 arc minutes per hour from 1975-1989. The analysis suggests that visual motion detection is possible in under an hour, while photographic detection requires specific focal lengths and exposure times to show streaking.

articles.title: VISUALLY OBSERVING THE HORSEHEAD
articles.summary: Stephen R. Waldee recounts his persistent and ultimately successful quest to visually observe the elusive Horsehead Nebula (Barnard 33). Initially failing with large instruments due to light pollution and inexperience, he eventually discerned the nebula under darker skies, employing various telescopes, H-Beta and UltraBlock filters, and focused observing techniques. His experience highlights the challenge of this observation and the satisfaction derived from dedicated deep-sky viewing.

articles.title: OFFICERS AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
articles.summary: This document lists the current officers and board of directors, including their respective titles such as President, Vice President, Treasurer, Secretary, and Editor. Each individual's name is provided along with a contact phone number, detailing the leadership structure of the organization.

articles.title: COMET EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: This document provides detailed ephemeris data for two comets, Helin-Roman-Alu (1989v) and Aarseth-Brewington (1989al). It lists their celestial coordinates (RA and DEC for both 1950 and 2000 epochs), elongation from the Sun, sky visibility, and predicted magnitude across various dates from December to February. This information is crucial for observers tracking these celestial objects.

articles.title: JUPITER'S RED SPOT
articles.summary: This document provides a detailed schedule for observing Jupiter's Great Red Spot (GRS) as it transits the central meridian. The times, presented in Pacific Standard Time (PST), cover observation opportunities from late December to early February. This resource is designed to assist astronomers and sky-watchers in planning their observations of the prominent Jovian feature.

articles.title: ASTRO ADS
articles.summary: This document, titled 'ASTRO ADS', serves as a free classifieds section for non-commercial advertisers selling astronomically related products and services. It lists various used telescopes, such as Meade and Celestron models, along with accessories like eyepieces, filters, mounts, and even a collection of Sky & Telescope magazines. Each ad includes a description of the item, asking price, and contact information for potential buyers.

articles.title: SPACE PROGRAM UPDATE
articles.summary: This space program update details several ongoing missions and upcoming events from late 1989. It covers the successful completion of a Space Shuttle Discovery mission, the upcoming Columbia launch, and the deployment of the COBE satellite to study cosmic background radiation. Additionally, it provides an update on the Galileo Jupiter spacecraft's first course correction and fuel status, mentions Geosat's measurement of Earth's geoid, and reports a delay in the first Pegasus air-launched booster flight test.

articles.title: EXPECTATIONS FOR HIPPARCOS SATELLITE INCREASED
articles.summary: Expectations for the European Hipparcos satellite have increased despite its initial elliptical orbit due to a motor failure. Successful perigee raising, increased ground station tracking, and sufficient power during eclipses suggest it will now last longer and complete more of its mission. The article also includes news on the Soviet space program, noting the Kvant-2 module docking with Mir and the launch of the Granat astronomy satellite.

articles.title: MORE FROM THE COSMIC MIND BOGGLING BOOK
articles.summary: This article presents fascinating facts about various extreme celestial objects. It highlights the incredible density of Sirius B, a white dwarf nearly as massive as the Sun, and theorizes that some white dwarfs may be Earth-sized diamonds. The piece also describes the immense density of neutron stars, where a pinhead of material would weigh a million tons.

articles.title: EPHEMERIS
articles.summary: EPHEMERIS is the monthly publication of the San Jose Astronomical Association, providing essential contact information for both the association and its editor. Members are invited to contribute articles, with a submission deadline of the 12th of the preceding month.

articles.title: MEMBERSHIP ONLY: $10    MEMBERSHIP/S&T: $26    JUNIOR (UNDER 18): $18
articles.summary: This document outlines the membership options and fees for the San Jose Astronomical Association (SJAA), including different tiers for membership only, membership with Sky & Telescope magazine, and junior members. It provides a form for new or renewal applications, including payment instructions and mailing address for the treasurer.
